text: WhatsApp Messenger, commonly known as WhatsApp, is an American social media, instant messaging (IM), and Voice over IP (VoIP) service accessible via desktop and mobile apps. Owned by Meta Platforms, it enables users to send text messages, voice messages, and video messages, make voice and video calls, and share images, documents, user locations, and other content. The service requires a cellular mobile telephone number to register and was launched in May 2009. It was founded by Brian Acton and Jan Koum, former Yahoo! employees, who incorporated WhatsApp Inc. in California on February 24, 2009, after Koum purchased an iPhone and decided to create an app for the App Store. The idea initially involved displaying statuses in a phone's Contacts menu to show if someone was at work or on a call. Their discussions took place at the home of Koum's Russian friend Alex Fishman in West San Jose, where Fishman introduced Igor Solomennikov, a Russian developer, to Koum. Koum named the app WhatsApp to sound like "what's up" and it was published on the Apple App Store in May 2009 and on BlackBerry App World in June 2009. Early versions of the app crashed, leading Koum to consider quitting, but Acton encouraged him to wait. In June 2009, Apple introduced push technology, prompting Koum to update WhatsApp so that users in a network would be notified when a status changed, which users began using to send jokey custom statuses like "I woke up late" or "I'm on my way," leading Fishman to say it "sort of became instant messaging." WhatsApp 2.0, released for iPhone in August 2009, included a purpose-designed messaging component and increased active users to 250,000. Acton joined WhatsApp in November 2009 after persuading five former Yahoo! friends to invest $250,000 in seed funding. Koum hired Chris Peiffer to develop a BlackBerry version, which arrived two months later. WhatsApp for Symbian OS was added in May 2010, and for Android OS in August 2010. Google made multiple acquisition offers for WhatsApp in 2010, which were declined. To cover verification text costs, WhatsApp transitioned from a free to a paid service. In December 2009, photo sending was added to the iOS version, and by early 2011, WhatsApp was among the top 20 apps in the U.S. Apple App Store. In April 2011, Sequoia Capital invested $8 million for over 15% of the company. By February 2013, WhatsApp had 200 million active users and 50 staff members, with Sequoia investing another $50 million at a $1.5 billion valuation. In 2013, WhatsApp acquired SkyMobius, the developers of Vtok, a video and voice calling app. As of December 2013, the service had 400 million monthly active users and incurred $148 million in expenses with a net loss of $138 million. On February 19, 2014, Facebook (now Meta Platforms) acquired WhatsApp for approximately US$19.3 billion, its largest acquisition to date, and the largest acquisition of a venture-capital-backed company in history. Sequoia Capital received an approximate 5,000% return on its initial investment. Facebook paid $4 billion in cash, $12 billion in Facebook shares, and $3 billion in restricted stock units to WhatsApp's founders Koum and Acton, with employee stock vesting over four years. Days after the announcement, WhatsApp users experienced a service loss, causing anger on social media. The acquisition was influenced by data from Facebook's Onavo app, which monitored competitor usage and performance. The acquisition led many users to try or switch to other messaging services, with Telegram gaining 8 million new users and Line gaining 2 million. At a Mobile World Congress keynote in February 2014, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg linked the acquisition to Facebook's Internet.org vision, proposing a bundle of free basic internet services like messaging as a "911 for the internet" to encourage users to pay for data services. Three days after the announcement, Koum stated that voice calls would be introduced, that new mobile phones would be sold in Germany with the WhatsApp brand, and that the ultimate goal was to be on all smartphones. In August 2014, WhatsApp became the world's most popular messaging app with over 600 million users. By early January 2015, it had 700 million monthly users and over 30 billion messages daily. In April 2015, Forbes predicted the telecommunications industry would lose $386 billion between 2012 and 2018 due to "over-the-top" services like WhatsApp and Skype. By April 2015, WhatsApp had over 800 million users. By September 2015, it reached 900 million users, and by February 2016, it surpassed one billion. On November 30, 2015, the Android WhatsApp client made links to Telegram unclickable and not copyable, an intentional implementation due to the presence of "telegram" in the code, which some viewed as an anti-competitive measure. On January 18, 2016, co-founder Jan Koum announced the removal of a $1 annual subscription fee to remove a barrier for users without payment cards, and stated that the app would not display third-party ads and would introduce features for communicating with businesses. In May 2017, the European Commission fined Facebook €110 million for "providing misleading information" about the WhatsApp takeover in 2014, claiming Facebook falsely stated it was technically impossible to combine user data from Facebook and WhatsApp. However, by summer 2016, WhatsApp had begun sharing user information with Facebook, allowing phone numbers to be used for targeted ads. Facebook acknowledged the breach but said the 2014 errors were not intentional. In September 2017, co-founder Brian Acton left WhatsApp to start the Signal Foundation, a nonprofit that developed the Signal messaging app. WhatsApp also announced a business platform to enable companies to provide customer service at scale, with airlines KLM and Aeroméxico participating in testing. In January 2018, WhatsApp launched WhatsApp Business for small business use. In April 2018, co-founder and CEO Jan Koum announced he would leave the company, citing concerns about privacy, advertising, and monetization by Facebook. Initially, it was believed that Acton and Koum gave up $1.3 billion in unvested stock options, but it was later reported that Koum retained $450 million via a "rest and vest" program. Facebook named Chris Daniels as Koum's replacement. On November 25, 2019, WhatsApp announced a $250,000 investment through a partnership with Startup India to provide 500 startups with $500 in Facebook ad credits each. In December 2019, WhatsApp updated its app to require Apple users to have iOS 9 or higher and Samsung, Huawei, Sony, and Google users to have version 4.0 by February 1, 2020, and announced that Windows Phone support would end after December 31, 2019. WhatsApp was announced as the third most downloaded mobile phone app of the 2010–2019 decade. In March 2020, WhatsApp partnered with the World Health Organization and UNICEF to provide messaging hotlines for COVID-19 information and began testing a feature to help users verify information to combat misinformation. In January 2021, WhatsApp introduced a controversial new privacy policy allowing data sharing with its parent company, Facebook, leading many users to delete the app and switch to Signal and Telegram. The policy does not apply in the EU due to violations of GDPR. Facing criticism, WhatsApp postponed the update to May 15, 2021, and had no plans to limit functionality or nag users who did not accept the new terms. The 2021 Facebook outage affected Instagram and WhatsApp. In May 2022, WhatsApp launched its Cloud API services (now known as WhatsApp Business Platform) for larger businesses, enabling integration with other software, a central account for multiple users, and advanced automation. In August 2022, WhatsApp launched an integration with JioMart, available only in India, allowing users to text special numbers to launch in-app grocery orders. In March 2024, Meta announced that WhatsApp would allow third-party messaging services to enable interoperability with WhatsApp, as required by the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA), allowing users to send messages between other apps and WhatsApp while maintaining end-to-end encryption. On February 24, 2017, WhatsApp launched a Status feature similar to Snapchat and Facebook stories. In 2023, WhatsApp introduced a "Voice Status Update" feature allowing users to record voice notes and share them as their status. In December 2021, WhatsApp changed the default setting for hiding online status from "everyone" to only contacts or those who have conversed with the user ("nobody" is also an option). In 2022, users could turn off their online status. In October 2018, the "Swipe to Reply" option was added to the Android beta version, 16 months after its iOS introduction. In early 2020, WhatsApp launched a "dark mode" for iPhone and Android devices. In October 2020, users could mute individuals and group chats forever with options of "8 hours," "1 week," and "Always," replacing the original "1 year" option. In May 2023, WhatsApp allowed users to edit messages within a 15-minute window after sending, with edited messages tagged as "edited," and introduced text formatting options like code blocks, quote blocks, and bulleted lists. In October 2024, WhatsApp expanded its chat filter feature to allow users to create custom lists of specific chats. In August 2013, WhatsApp added voice messages to its apps. Voice calls between two accounts were added in March and April 2015, with over 100 million voice calls per day reported by June 2016. In November 2016, video calls between two accounts were introduced. In September 2018, group audio and video call features were added. In July 2023, video messages were introduced, allowing users to record and send short videos directly in chats, limited to 60 seconds. In November 2023, WhatsApp added a "voice chat" feature for groups with more than 32 members, where participants receive a notification to join rather than being directly called. In December 2023, the "View Once" feature expanded to include voice messages, which are deleted after the first listen. In June 2024, improvements to voice and video calls allowed up to 32 participants in video calls, added audio to screen sharing, and introduced a new codec to increase call reliability. In November 2024, the ability to transcribe voice messages was added, allowing users to read out what was said. In December 2024, WhatsApp introduced features allowing users to select specific participants from a group to make a call and added visual effects to video feeds. In November 2010, iOS improvements included message search, trimming long videos, canceling media uploads/downloads, and previewing photos before sending. In March 2012, WhatsApp enhanced its location-sharing function to allow users to share not only their location but also other details.

In June 2024, WhatsApp improved voice and video calls by allowing up to 32 participants in video calls, adding audio to screen sharing, and introducing a new codec to enhance call reliability. In November 2024, the app added the ability to transcribe voice messages so users can read the content instead of listening to the audio. In December 2024, new video calling features were introduced, including the option to select specific participants from a group rather than calling all members, and visual effects were added to enhance the video feed. In November 2010, iOS version updates included message search in chat history, trimming long videos to sendable sizes, canceling media during upload or download, and previewing photos before sending. In March 2012, location-sharing was enhanced to allow users to share not only their location but also that of places like restaurants or hotels. In July 2017, WhatsApp added support for uploading files of all types with a 100 MB limit, previously restricting uploads to images (JPG, PNG, GIF), videos (MP4, AVI), and documents (CSV, DOC/DOCX, PDF, PPT/PPTX, RTF, TXT, XLS/XLSX). In July 2021, the app announced upcoming support for sending uncompressed images and videos in three quality options: Auto, Best Quality, and Data Saver. In May 2022, the file upload limit increased to 2 GB, and the maximum group size was raised to 512 members. On November 10, 2016, a beta version of two-factor authentication for Android users was launched using email addresses for added security, and Facebook ceased collecting WhatsApp data for advertising in Europe. In October 2019, WhatsApp introduced a fingerprint app-locking feature for Android users. In July 2021, the company announced forthcoming support for end-to-end encryption for backups stored in Facebook's cloud. In August 2021, a feature allowing chat history transfer between mobile operating systems was launched, initially on Samsung phones with plans to expand to Android and iOS soon. In October 2023, passkey support was introduced, enabling users to verify login with on-device biometrics instead of SMS, and in November 2023, support for sending login codes to a linked email address instead of SMS was added. On November 30, a Secret Code feature was introduced, allowing users of locked chats to enter a unique password to hide those chats from view when unlocking the app. In January 2015, a web client was launched that allowed users to scan a QR code to mirror their chats in a browser, requiring the phone to stay connected and not available for iOS initially due to Apple limitations. Since then, linked devices support has expanded. In July 2021, multi-device support was tested, allowing computer users to run WhatsApp without an active phone session. In April 2023, the app rolled out account access across multiple phones, introducing Companion mode for Android users to link up to five phones and later expanding to iOS users to link up to four iPhones. In October 2023, support for logging into two accounts within the same app was added. On October 25, 2018, WhatsApp announced support for Stickers, requiring third-party apps to add them. In March 2021, third-party animated stickers were rolled out first in Iran, Brazil, and Indonesia, then globally. In December 2022, WhatsApp launched 3D digital avatars usable as profile pictures or stickers, similar to Bitmoji or Memoji. In April 2022, WhatsApp announced plans for a Communities feature allowing multiple group chats in a shared space with unified notifications and smaller discussion groups, as well as reactions, message deletion by administrators, and voice calls up to 32 participants. In June 2023, WhatsApp Channels was launched, enabling content creators and organizations to send newsletter-like broadcasts to large audiences, with channels not being end-to-end encrypted; initially available in Colombia and Singapore, then Egypt, Chile, Malaysia, Morocco, Ukraine, Kenya, and Peru, becoming widely available in September 2023. In April 2024, an AI-powered "Smart Assistant" based on the LLaMa 3 model became widely available, allowing users to ask questions or generate images, and was also available on Facebook and Instagram; chat filters were introduced to sort chats by All, Unread, or Groups. In September 2024, support for Meta AI was expanded, allowing users to send text and photos to Meta AI to ask questions, identify objects, translate text, or edit pictures. In December 2024, a reverse image search feature was introduced, enabling users to verify image authenticity using Google Search. In November 2025, WhatsApp updated its About feature to allow users to add a short message explaining their activities, which defaults to disappearing after 24 hours but can be set for longer and restricted to specific contacts; the update was introduced for the Christmas period to inform contacts of holiday activities, as the feature was previously hidden and difficult to find. Currently, WhatsApp's principal platforms are Android and iPhones, requiring at least Android 5.0 or iOS 15.1 as of 2025. Linked devices, which sync with a primary phone, support up to four devices per account and automatically log out after 14 days of inactivity; they enable use on desktops, smartwatches, and other smartphones (companions). Originally, the primary phone had to remain online for linked devices to function, but as of an update in October 2021 and integrated by default in April 2022, this is no longer required. Multi-device support began testing in July 2021 and was fully rolled out in April 2023. WhatsApp Web, launched on January 21, 2015, allows users to access chats via web.whatsapp.com by scanning a QR code, initially available for Android, BlackBerry, Windows Phone, and later iOS, Nokia Series 40, and S60; previously, the handset had to stay connected, but this requirement was removed in October 2021 and became default in April 2022. When first introduced, the web version only showed messages from the last three months; since full rollout, users cannot access older messages. Unofficial versions for macOS, such as ChitChat (formerly WhatsMac), exist. On May 10, 2016, WhatsApp was released for Windows and macOS, supporting video and voice calls from desktop clients, compatible with Windows 8 and OS X 10.10 and higher. In 2023, WhatsApp replaced Electron-based apps with native versions for each platform, with the Windows version based on UWP and the Mac version using Catalyst technology. In July 2025, WhatsApp stopped developing the Windows UWP app due to poor support and Microsoft's deprecation of UWP, transitioning to the Microsoft Edge WebView2 framework, which has been criticized for sluggish performance, high RAM usage, and requiring background running for push notifications. WhatsApp was officially supported for iPads and iPadOS starting May 27, 2025, functioning as a linked device syncing with a smartphone. Support for Android Wear (now Wear OS) was added in 2014. WhatsApp uses a customized version of XMPP, specifically named "FunXMPP," as confirmed in a 2019 DOJ document related to a lawsuit against the NSO Group; upon installation, it creates a user account using the phone number as the Jabber ID (e.g., [phone number]@s.whatsapp.net). WhatsApp automatically adds contacts from the device's address book to the user's contact list by comparing phone numbers with its database. Previously, Android and Nokia Series 40 versions used an MD5-hashed, reversed IMEI as a password, while iOS used the Wi-Fi MAC address; a 2012 update introduced server-generated random passwords. Users can also contact others via https://api.whatsapp.com/send/?phone=[phone number]. Some dual-SIM devices may not be compatible, though unofficial workarounds exist. In February 2015, WhatsApp introduced voice calling, which helped attract new users; its voice codec is Opus, using MDCT and LPC compression at 8–16 kHz sampling rates. On November 14, 2016, video calling was added for Android, iPhone, and Windows Phone users. In November 2017, users were given seven minutes to delete messages sent by mistake. Multimedia messages are sent by uploading content to an HTTP server and sending a link with a Base64-encoded thumbnail if applicable. WhatsApp uses a "store and forward" mechanism where messages are stored on servers, repeatedly requested for acknowledgment, and deleted upon receipt or after 30 days if undelivered. On November 18, 2014, Open Whisper Systems partnered with WhatsApp to implement end-to-end encryption using the Signal Protocol; support for Android was confirmed, with plans for other clients, group messages, and key verification. In April 2015, Heise security confirmed Android-to-Android messages were encrypted, but iPhone messages were not, raising concerns about user awareness. On April 5, 2016, WhatsApp and Open Whisper Systems announced full end-to-end encryption for all communication, including key verification and a trust on first use option; messages are encrypted with the Signal Protocol, calls with SRTP, and client-server communications are layered in an encrypted channel. On October 14, 2021, end-to-end encryption for backups on Android and iOS was rolled out, requiring user activation and offering password or 64-digit key encryption. The app can store encrypted messages on SD cards, but chat messages are also stored unencrypted in the SQLite database file "msgstore.db". WhatsApp uses the Sender Keys protocol. WhatsApp Payments (WhatsApp Pay) became available in India, Brazil, and Singapore for business transactions. In July 2017, WhatsApp received permission from NPCI to partner with Indian banks for UPI-based transactions; UPI payments were initially limited to 20 million users in November 2020, expanded to 100 million in April 2022, and became generally available to all users in August 2022. On February 28, 2019, The New York Times reported Facebook's plan to develop an in-house cryptocurrency, "Facebook coin," later renamed Diem in December 2020, with a stablecoin pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, intended to be integrated into WhatsApp and Facebook via a digital wallet named Calibra, later rebranded to Novi in May 2020. Meta ended the Novi project on September 1, 2022. WhatsApp has repeatedly imposed message forwarding limits to combat misinformation in countries like India and Australia, first introduced in 2018 to fight spam, expanded in 2021, and stated to have helped curb the spread of false information about COVID-19.

A digital currency project initially proposed by former PayPal president David A. Marcus, known as the "Facebook coin," was intended to be a stablecoin pegged to a basket of foreign currencies. In June 2019, Facebook announced the project would be named Libra, with a digital wallet called Calibra to be integrated into Facebook and WhatsApp. Following regulatory concerns, Facebook rebranded the currency as Diem in December 2020 and introduced requirements for government-issued ID verification and fraud protection; Calibra was rebranded to Novi in May 2020. Meta (formerly Facebook) officially ended the Novi project on September 1, 2022. WhatsApp has implemented message forwarding limits since 2018 to combat misinformation, particularly in India and Australia, and these measures were expanded and remained active through 2021, helping to reduce the spread of false information about COVID-19. In India, after incidents involving fraudulent and violent messages falsely accusing individuals of abducting children, WhatsApp encouraged users to report such content and introduced labels for forwarded messages. In Brazil, WhatsApp was found to be abused for spreading fake news during the 2018 presidential elections, with US$3 million spent on illegal concealed contributions. Researchers and journalists urged Facebook to adopt India-style restrictions on hoaxes. Initially criticized for lacking encryption, WhatsApp introduced end-to-end encryption in April 2016 after a two-year process, earning a 6 out of 7 rating on the Electronic Frontier Foundation's Secure Messaging Scorecard in May 2016. However, it was criticized for backups not being end-to-end encrypted, allowing third-party access. In May 2019, a vulnerability allowed remote installation of spyware via unanswered calls; in September 2019, a 'delete for everyone' feature failed to remove media saved to the iOS camera roll due to Apple's security layers. In November 2019, WhatsApp introduced a feature allowing users to control who can add them to groups. In December 2019, a flaw enabled hackers to access data through malicious GIF files, which was patched and users were urged to update. A separate security flaw in September 2019 allowed cyber attackers to crash group chats, requiring app uninstall and reinstall, fixed in version 2.19.246 onwards. Since February 1, 2020, WhatsApp has been unavailable on smartphones using outdated operating systems like Android 2.3.7 or older and iPhone iOS 8 or older. In April 2020, the NSO Group claimed WhatsApp's lawsuit threatened its clients' national security and foreign policy, with end users including Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kazakhstan, Morocco, Mexico, and the UAE. On December 16, 2020, a claim surfaced in an anti-trust case against Google that WhatsApp gave Google access to private messages, though the details were redacted. In January 2021, WhatsApp announced a new privacy policy allowing data sharing with Facebook and its "family of companies" starting February 2021, removing the previous opt-out option, which was not applied in the EU due to GDPR. The enforcement was postponed to May 15, 2021, and WhatsApp stated it had no plans to limit app functionality for users who did not accept the terms. In October 2021, WhatsApp introduced end-to-end encryption for chat backups stored on Apple iCloud or Google Drive. In November 2021, an FBI document revealed WhatsApp responds to law enforcement warrants within minutes, providing metadata such as contact and address book information. In January 2022, an unsealed surveillance application revealed WhatsApp tracked seven users from China and Macau based on a US DEA request, collecting data on contacts and usage, without probable cause or identity linkage. In early 2022, Boldend, a San Diego startup founded in 2017 and partly financed by Peter Thiel, was found to have developed tools to hack WhatsApp's encryption, with the vulnerability patched in January 2021. In September 2022, a critical integer overflow bug in WhatsApp's Android video call feature allowed full control of a victim's app during a call, patched on the day it was reported. In 2025, WhatsApp alerted 90 journalists and civil society members to spyware attacks by Israeli company Paragon Solutions. In April 2025, Austrian researchers extracted 3.5 billion users' phone numbers through high-volume contact discovery requests, a flaw previously warned about in 2017, which was later addressed by Meta in October. As of 2023, WhatsApp is widely used by UK government institutions, though its use is seen as problematic due to hindering transparency, as officials may avoid official channels to evade scrutiny. The Information Commissioner has stated that WhatsApp use risks transparency, and transparency campaigners have challenged it in court. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the UK government used WhatsApp on personal devices to manage the crisis; when the official inquiry began in May 2023, a security breach compromised the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson's personal device, and the High Court ruled that all requested documents must be handed over unredacted. In 2018, around 500,000 NHS staff used WhatsApp at work, with 29,000 facing disciplinary action, despite policy prohibitions. In March 2019, WhatsApp issued a guide warning users against unofficial modified versions, stating such users may be banned. In May 2019, hackers using an NSO Group-developed exploit injected malware via WhatsApp Voice over IP calls, targeting at least 100 human rights defenders, journalists, and civil society members across 20 countries. In October 2019, WhatsApp filed a lawsuit against NSO Group in San Francisco, alleging violations of US laws including the CFAA. In July 2020, a US federal judge ruled the lawsuit could proceed, rejecting NSO Group's motion to dismiss. In January 2020, a digital forensic analysis revealed Jeff Bezos received an encrypted message from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, which contained a malicious file leading to a phone hack, confirmed by UN special rapporteurs David Kaye and Agnes Callamard as part of a Saudi hit list targeting Jamal Khashoggi. In 2021, an FBI document obtained via a Freedom of Information request revealed WhatsApp and iMessage are vulnerable to real-time law-enforcement searches. In January 2022, The Wire reported that the BJP allegedly used an app called Tek Fog to hack inactive WhatsApp accounts to send propaganda, with a whistleblower able to hack a test account within minutes; Meta staff were later found to have been duped, and the report issued a formal apology. In December 2015, ISIS was reported to have used WhatsApp to plan the November 2015 Paris attacks and to traffic sex slaves. In March 2017, British Home Secretary Amber Rudd criticized WhatsApp's encryption, citing its use by Khalid Masood before the 2017 Westminster attack, and called for police access to encrypted messaging. In April 2017, the perpetrator of the Stockholm truck attack reportedly used WhatsApp to exchange messages with an ISIS supporter discussing explosive devices and confessing to the attack. In April 2017, nearly 300 WhatsApp groups with about 250 members each were used to mobilize stone-pelters in Jammu and Kashmir, with 90% closed after police contacted admins; a six-month probe found 1000 members and admins from Pakistan and Gulf nations, with funding from barter trade. In May 2022, the FBI arrested an ISIS sympathizer plotting to assassinate George W. Bush based on WhatsApp data, with the account under surveillance. Numerous scams on WhatsApp spread viruses or malware, including a 2016 scam involving WhatsApp Gold, which infected users with malware; a message promising access to friends' conversations or contact lists became popular in Brazil, leading to over 1.5 million users clicking and losing money since December 2016. GB WhatsApp is considered malicious by Symantec due to unauthorized device operations. WhatsApp is owned by Meta, whose Facebook service has been blocked in China since 2009; in September 2017, WhatsApp was reported to be completely blocked in China, and on April 19, 2024, Apple removed WhatsApp from the App Store in China due to government orders on national security grounds. In May 2014, Iran proposed blocking WhatsApp, citing Mark Zuckerberg's perceived political affiliations, and the block was permanently enforced until Meta responded in September 2022. Turkey temporarily banned WhatsApp in 2016 after the assassination of the Russian ambassador. In March 2016, Facebook vice-president Diego Dzodan was arrested in Brazil for not cooperating with a court request for WhatsApp conversations, but was released the next day due to a disproportionate and unreasonable arrest. On May 2, 2016, Brazilian mobile providers were ordered to block WhatsApp for 72 hours for the second time for failing to comply with court orders, with the block lifted after less than 24 hours. On June 23, 2020, Brazil's Central Bank ordered Visa and Mastercard to stop working with WhatsApp on its electronic payment system, citing the need to preserve a competitive, secure, transparent, open, and affordable payment environment.

On March 1, 2016, Diego Dzodan, Facebook's vice-president for Latin America, was arrested in Brazil for not cooperating with an investigation involving requests for WhatsApp conversations. On March 2, 2016, at dawn, he was released by the Court of Appeal, which ruled the arrest was disproportionate and unreasonable. On May 2, 2016, Brazilian mobile providers were ordered to block WhatsApp for 72 hours due to the service's second failure to comply with criminal court orders; the block was lifted after less than 24 hours following an appeal. On June 23, 2020, Brazil's Central Bank issued an order to Visa and Mastercard to cease working with WhatsApp on its new electronic payment system, citing the need to "preserve an adequate competitive environment" and ensure "functioning of a payment system that's interchangeable, fast, secure, transparent, open and cheap." The government of Uganda banned WhatsApp and Facebook, along with other social media platforms, to enforce a daily tax of USh.200/= on users, as established by parliament. The United Arab Emirates banned WhatsApp video chat and VoIP call applications as early as 2013, reportedly to protect the commercial interests of domestic telecom providers du and Etisalat, with reports suggesting ToTok can spy on users. In July 2021, the Cuban government blocked access to several social media platforms, including WhatsApp, to limit the spread of information during anti-government protests. In December 2021, the Swiss army banned the use of WhatsApp and other non-Swiss encrypted messaging services by personnel due to concerns over U.S. authorities accessing user data under the CLOUD Act, recommending instead the use of Threema, a Swiss-based service. In August 2021, Access Now reported that WhatsApp and other social media apps were blocked in Zambia during the general election, with a significant drop in traffic, though the government made no official statement. The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) prohibited local banks from using instant messaging apps like WhatsApp for customer communication to enhance data security and protect customer information. On November 28, 2025, Russia threatened a full ban on WhatsApp. In mid-2013, WhatsApp Inc. filed for DMCA takedown of a discussion thread on the XDA Developers forums about the third-party client "WhatsApp Plus." In 2015, third-party clients reverse-engineering the WhatsApp app received cease and desist orders, leading to bans for their users. In January 2018, WhatsApp launched two business-oriented apps, with the on-premise version later deprecated and fully sunset on October 23, 2025, while the WhatsApp Cloud API became available in 2022. Businesses must subscribe through Meta's approved Business Solution Providers, such as respond.io, Gupshup, Trengo, Wati, and Manychat. In October 2020, Facebook introduced pricing tiers for the WhatsApp Business API based on per-conversation charges; on July 1, 2025, a new tier system came into effect charging per-message instead. WhatsApp handled ten billion messages per day in August 2012, growing from two billion in April 2012 and one billion the previous October, reaching 27 billion messages on June 13, 2013, with the Financial Times noting it "has done to SMS on mobile phones what Skype did to international calling on landlines." By April 22, 2014, WhatsApp had over 500 million monthly active users, with 700 million photos and 100 million videos shared daily, handling more than 10 billion messages each day. On August 24, 2014, Koum announced WhatsApp had over 600 million active users worldwide, adding about 25 million new users monthly, or 833,000 active users per day. In May 2017, it was reported that WhatsApp users spent over 340 million minutes on video calls daily, equivalent to roughly 646 years of video calls per day. By February 2017, WhatsApp had over 1.2 billion users globally, reaching 1.5 billion monthly active users by the end of 2017. In January 2020, WhatsApp surpassed 5 billion installs on Google Play Store, becoming only the second non-Google app to do so. In February 2020, WhatsApp had over 2 billion users globally. In May 2025, Meta reported WhatsApp had over 3 billion monthly active users globally. India is WhatsApp's largest market by total users; in May 2014, it crossed 50 million monthly active users, reaching 70 million in October 2014, making up 10% of WhatsApp's total user base, and by February 2017, it reached 200 million monthly active users. Israel is one of WhatsApp's strongest markets, with 92% of smartphones having the app installed by 2013 and 86% of users reporting daily use. In July 2024, WhatsApp reached 100 million users in the United States. WhatsApp competes with messaging services including iMessage (1.3 billion active users), WeChat (1.26 billion), Telegram (900 million), Viber (260 million), LINE (217 million), KakaoTalk (57 million), and Signal (70 million), with Telegram and Signal experiencing registration spikes during WhatsApp outages and controversies. WhatsApp has increasingly drawn innovation from competing services, such as a Telegram-inspired web version and group features, and in 2016 was accused of copying features from an unreleased version of iMessage.
